passages.happening:
David's son Amnon falls in love, as the text puts it, with Tamar, the beautiful sister of his half-brother Absalom. He is sick with frustration over her, ‘for she was a virgin, and it seemed implausible for him to do anything to her’ (verse 2).

His cousin Jonadab, ‘a very shrewd man’ (verse 3), gives him a plan. Amnon is to lie in bed and pretend to be ill, and when the king comes, ask for Tamar to come and cook for him. Amnon does it, and David sends word to Tamar: “Please go to the house of Amnon your brother and prepare a meal for him” (verse 7).

Tamar goes. She kneads dough and bakes cakes where he can see her. He refuses to eat, sends everyone out, and tells her to bring the food into the bedroom. There he seizes her and demands that she lie with him.

“No, my brother!” she cried. “Do not humiliate me, for such a thing should never be done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing! Where could I ever take my shame? And you would be like one of the fools in Israel! Please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you” (verses 12-13).

‘But Amnon refused to listen to her, and being stronger, he violated her and lay with her’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Nathan had said that the sword would never leave David's house and that evil would rise against him from within it. This is the first fulfillment.

Amnon is David's firstborn, by Ahinoam of Jezreel, and so the natural heir. Absalom is the third son, by Maacah, the daughter of the king of Geshur. Tamar is Absalom's full sister and Amnon's half-sister.

The text calls what Amnon feels love, and then shows what it was. Jonadab supplies the plan, and the king himself is used to deliver Tamar. The law of Moses forbade a man to take his half-sister. Tamar's plea that the king would not withhold her may reflect an older custom, since Abraham married his half-sister, or it may simply be her desperate attempt to get out of the room. Her words, such a thing should never be done in Israel, are the words used of the rape of Dinah and of the crime at Gibeah. The word she uses, humiliate, is the word the chapter uses for what Amnon did to her. It names forced degradation for what it is.

The chapter is told with painful restraint. It lets the characters' words show who they are: Jonadab's cunning, Amnon's commands, Tamar's reasoned and dignified pleading. Again and again she is called his sister, keeping the family bond in view as it is violated.
passages.later:
The law Tamar appeals to is plain: ‘You must not have sexual relations with your sister, either your father’s daughter or your mother’s daughter’ (Leviticus 18:9).

Her cry echoes the story of Dinah, when her brothers heard that Shechem had committed ‘an outrage in Israel’ (Genesis 34:7), and the crime at Gibeah, which the Levite called ‘a lewd and disgraceful act in Israel’ (Judges 20:6).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible tell this story?

The Bible does not hide sexual violence, even in the king's own family, and it tells Tamar's story with all its sympathy on her side. She is given the chapter's clearest moral voice. She names the act as a wrong, appeals to what should never be done in Israel and to Amnon's own good, and even offers him a way out. He will not listen.

The wrong was Amnon's alone, and the shame Tamar feared belonged to him, not to her. The story is not told as an example to follow. It is told so that the wrong is named and seen, and so that a reader can understand what follows in David's house.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Amnon's love turned to hatred within the hour. Ask what the difference is between love and the wish to possess. And ask how you can make it safe for the people around you to say no, and be heard.

passages.happening:
‘Then Amnon hated Tamar with such intensity that his hatred was greater than the love he previously had’ (verse 15). He orders her out. “No,” she replied, “sending me away is worse than this great wrong you have already done to me!” (verse 16). He will not listen. He has his servant throw her out and bolt the door.

Tamar is wearing a long robe of many colors, the dress of the king's virgin daughters. She puts ashes on her head, tears the robe, and goes away crying bitterly, her hand on her head (verses 18-19).

Her brother Absalom says to her, “Has your brother Amnon been with you? Be quiet for now, my sister. He is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart” (verse 20). ‘So Tamar lived as a desolate woman in the house of her brother Absalom’ (verse 20).

“When King David heard all this, he was furious” (verse 21). Absalom never says a word to Amnon, good or bad, ‘because he hated Amnon for disgracing his sister Tamar’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Amnon's so-called love turns in a moment into a hatred greater than the love, and the turn shows that it was lust.

Tamar's words about being sent away need their background. The law required a man who violated an unmarried virgin to marry her and never divorce her, a protection for a woman's future in a world where she might otherwise be left with no household at all. By throwing her out, Amnon adds a second wrong to the first and leaves her with nothing. Nothing in this chapter, or in that law, teaches that a woman who has been raped should marry the man who did it. The notes on Deuteronomy 22 set out that law with its difficulties.

Her robe marked her as a king's daughter. The same rare phrase describes Joseph's robe, and in both stories a favored child's garment becomes part of a family coming apart. Ashes and torn clothes were signs of mourning and shame. Tamar does not hide what was done to her. She goes out crying aloud.

Then the men around her close in. Absalom, who loves her, tells her to be quiet because the man who harmed her is family, and she lives on, desolate, in his house. David, the king and her father, is furious, and does nothing. The Greek translation, and a fragment of Samuel among the Dead Sea Scrolls, add that he would not punish Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn. Either way the point stands. The king was angry, and he did not act.
passages.later:
Joseph's father had made him the same kind of garment: ‘so he made him a robe of many colors’ (Genesis 37:3).

David repeats an old failure. When Jacob heard that his daughter Dinah had been violated, ‘he remained silent about it until they returned’ (Genesis 34:5), and it was her brothers who acted.
passages.hard:
Why does David do nothing?

The text exposes David's failure. He was furious, but he did not punish his son, protect his daughter, or bring the matter to justice. Interpreters offer several reasons. He may have favored his firstborn, as the Greek text says. He may have felt his own authority weakened by his sin with Bathsheba. He may simply have been a passive father. The narrator does not excuse him, and the consequences of his inaction run through the rest of the book.

For readers who have suffered abuse, the chapter's honesty matters. Scripture names the wrong, believes the one who was harmed, and shows the damage done when those in power fail to act. It names the silence too. A house that protects the one who did harm instead of the one who was harmed has failed her.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Absalom told his sister to be quiet because the man who harmed her was family. Ask where you have heard that said, in a family or a church, and whom it protected. And ask what it would cost you to stand beside someone who has been told to keep quiet.

passages.happening:
Two years later Absalom holds a sheepshearing feast at Baal-hazor and invites all the king's sons. He asks the king to come too. David will not go, ‘but gave him his blessing’ (verse 25). Absalom asks that Amnon come, and the king sends Amnon with the rest of his sons.

Absalom orders his young men, ‘Watch Amnon until his heart is merry with wine, and when I order you to strike Amnon down, you are to kill him’ (verse 28). They do as he ordered, and the king's other sons flee on their mules.

A report reaches David that Absalom has killed all the king's sons. The king tears his clothes and lies on the ground. Then Jonadab, the cousin who had planned the first wrong, tells him that only Amnon is dead: ‘In fact, Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar’ (verse 32). The king's sons arrive, wailing, and the king and his servants weep bitterly.

Absalom flees to Talmai, the king of Geshur, his mother's father, and stays there three years. ‘But David mourned for his son every day’ (verse 37). ‘And King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon’s death’ (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
Sheepshearing was a festival with feasting and wine, like the feast Nabal was holding when David's men came to him (1 Samuel 25). Mules were royal mounts, which is why the king's sons flee on them.

The chapter mirrors David's own sin. In chapter 11 the king saw, desired, arranged and took, and then arranged a killing. Here a king's son sees, desires, arranges and takes, and then a brother arranges a killing at a feast where the victim's heart is merry with wine, as David once made Uriah drunk. Sin passes from one generation to the next.

With Amnon dead, and the second son, Chileab, never mentioned after 3:3, Absalom is now the likely heir. His revenge has a political edge as well as a personal one.

Notice how often David is told things and how rarely he acts. He hears of Tamar and is furious. He hears of Amnon and tears his clothes. Absalom flees, and David mourns, and longs, and does nothing. That passivity leads straight to the revolt that will drive him from Jerusalem.
passages.later: Dinah's brothers, too, took revenge for their sister with the sword: ‘two of Jacob’s sons (Dinah’s brothers Simeon and Levi) took their swords’ (Genesis 34:25).
passages.asks: David's failure to act left justice to Absalom's revenge. Ask where a wrong that was never faced has hardened into something worse. And ask what justice, done rightly and in time, might have spared.
